questions: Did this difficulty with walking start suddenly (over minutes to hours)?
Do you notice any tremor, especially at rest or when your hands are relaxed?
Have you experienced any numbness, tingling, or "pins and needles" in your feet or legs?
Have you had problems with your memory or thinking recently?
Do you have any difficulty controlling your bladder?
Does anyone in your family have problems with balance or walking?
Have you noticed your speech becoming slurred or difficult to understand?
Have you experienced any dizziness or nausea alongside these walking problems?
Do your symptoms get worse as you continue to walk and improve if you sit or lie down?
Have you had any recent falls, and if so, did they tend to be backward or in any particular direction?
Have you noticed your handwriting becoming smaller or more cramped recently?

results: 1. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with attention to the cerebellum and brainstem
brain MRI: cerebellar atrophy on sagittal T1 and axial FLAIR
2. Genetic testing for hereditary spinocerebellar ataxias, including Friedreich's ataxia GAA repeat expansion
genetic ataxia panel: 112 and 29 CTG repeats in ATXN8OS - confirms SCA8
copper / caeruloplasmin: normal - excludes Wilson disease
10. Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis
lumbar puncture / CSF: normal cells, protein and glucose; no oligoclonal bands
dx_raw:
DIAGNOS: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 8 (SCA8), caused by CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the ATXN8OS gene on chromosome 13q21, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern

Alternative diagnoses still considered:

1. Another autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia (e.g., SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA6) — though these were excluded by the genetic panel, phenotypic variability and incomplete penetrance can occasionally complicate interpretation
2. Multiple system atrophy, cerebellar type (MSA-C) — a sporadic neurodegenerative disorder that can present with progressive cerebellar ataxia and dysarthria, though the positive family history and normal autonomic function argue against this
3. Friedreich's ataxia — the most common inherited ataxia, though typically autosomal recessive with early onset, peripheral neuropathy, and absent reflexes, features not seen here; also excluded by genetic testing
order_raw:
1. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with attention to the cerebellum and brainstem
2. Genetic testing for hereditary spinocerebellar ataxias, including Friedreich's ataxia GAA repeat expansion
3. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography
4. Serum vitamin B12 level
5. Serum vitamin E level
6. Serum alpha-fetoprotein level
7. Complete blood count
8. Thyroid function tests
9. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels
10. Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis
dx: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 8 (SCA8), caused by CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the ATXN8OS gene on chromosome 13q21, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
